answer.rationale: The binding constraints are the 14-day expiry and 94% line utilization with zero buffer, so any action requiring qualification, onboarding, or migration work inside this cycle imports delivery risk that the 18% cost mandate does not justify. memory_c2 (switch to low-cost vendor) is the largest apparent cost lever and therefore the one most likely to be misapplied here: I verify it to see whether the original record involved a component with slack capacity and a long qualification runway, conditions that plainly do not hold now. memory_c4 (renegotiation with market benchmarking recovered price and payment terms) is the mechanism I actually intend to lean on, so I verify its source to confirm the recovered margin was real and durable rather than a one-cycle concession, and to see what leverage was used. memory_c6 suggests a multi-year commitment could unlock volume pricing, which is a plausible path to a meaningful share of the 18%, and memory_c1 supports incumbent continuity as low-risk. I therefore intend a guarded, narrow move: negotiate the incumbent renewal on benchmarked price and payment terms, structured short enough (or with an exit) to avoid locking in a long commitment before a second source can be qualified. Caveats I am explicitly holding open: every inherited memory records a success and none records a failure, so the archive is survivorship-biased and its base rates should not be treated as decision-grade; renegotiation alone may not reach 18%, which is a real shortfall risk I am accepting this cycle rather than papering over; and declining to add a second source (memory_c3) leaves a single point of failure that should be the first item at the next review. If verification shows memory_c4's savings were illusory or one-off, the fallback is a short-term extension (memory_c5) rather than a rushed vendor switch, since preserving optionality beats a migration into a no-buffer line.
